pages.title: Everything agent coordination concept
pages.markdown:
Everything gives users one or more named agents that do work on their behalf, stay highly responsive, and delegate heavily to dedicated “coding agents.” Communicating with a named agent should feel like texting a person: the user sees the messages the agent chooses to send, while its internal work happens in the background. Code changes, pull requests, and research are examples; the scope remains open.

[Architecture](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_2b6d7736601c8191bdf3ef991520ee7c)

[User Surfaces](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b5de4204a0808191a448e59fce061e9e)

## Fleet as the core orchestration layer

Fleet is the core orchestration layer for Everything. Main agents will use Fleet MCP to create agent workspaces, called instances in Fleet, and launch and control the dedicated agents they delegate work to. The main agent corresponds to Fleet's admiral.

Agent workspaces can use reusable workspace templates and include GitHub repositories where needed. Everything will build its delegation system on Fleet, making Fleet a foundational architectural choice.

## Asynchronous work and waking the main agent

Schedules, including cron jobs, and external events can start asynchronous work in dedicated agents running in Fleet instances. Fleet already supports starting instance work on a schedule.

A dedicated agent may choose to message the main agent, waking it to review the message and take action. The main agent can act in the background, delegate follow-up work through Fleet, and decide whether to contact the user through its messaging tool. This flow lets work progress without a new user message.

**Fleet dependency:** Messaging from an instance agent to the admiral is a Fleet capability still to be added. Everything's conceptual design assumes it is available; implementing that capability belongs to Fleet.

## Core interaction

Each named main agent runs its own work loop. Its turns do not automatically appear in the conversation. To communicate with the user, it must deliberately call a messaging tool.

The main agent stays engaged with the user while delegating heavily to dedicated “coding agents.” It can process updates and direct work without sending a message, then choose when to ask a question, share progress, deliver a result, or reply. The conversation should feel like an exchange of text messages. Sending a message need not end its work.

## Attention

When the user communicates, their message interrupts the main agent's current activity. The main agent must turn its attention to the user quickly and remain responsive throughout ongoing work.

Incoming user messages trigger that interruption. Outgoing messages remain deliberate actions through the messaging tool.

## Persistent storage and user artifacts

Each named main agent has a persistent filesystem for notes, remembered context, and other files it chooses to save. It can write information down and read it again across turns and wake-ups, giving it a durable place to keep memory and working context.

Alongside that storage, the main agent has an artifact directory for HTML files and supporting assets. A static web server, such as Nginx serving an HTML folder, makes those artifacts visible to the user. The agent can create and update pages the user can open and interact with.

Artifacts add a visual, interactive way to share work alongside the text-message conversation. The main agent can send artifact links through its messaging tool.

## Conceptual map

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    U["User"] -->|"User messages interrupt current activity"| C["Named main agent powered by Pi / Fleet admiral"]
    C -->|"Explicit tool call"| M["Send message to user"]
    M -->|"Reply, question, update, or result"| U
    C -->|"Delegate and control through Fleet MCP"| F["Fleet orchestration"]
    F -->|"Create instances, launch and control agents"| A["Dedicated coding agents / managed by Fleet in its instances"]
    S["Fleet schedules / cron jobs"] -->|"Start asynchronous work"| A
    E["External events"] -->|"Start asynchronous work"| A
    A -->|"May send a message to the main agent"| F
    F -->|"Deliver message and wake main agent"| C
    T["Workspace templates"] -.->|"Reusable instance setup"| F
    R["GitHub repositories"] -.->|"Included where needed"| A
    C <-->|"Read and write"| P["Persistent filesystem / notes and memory"]
    C -->|"Write and update"| H["Artifact directory / HTML files and assets"]
    H -->|"Serve to the user via Nginx or similar"| U
    C -->|"Process events and take action"| C
```

Pi is the chosen harness for the main agents only. Everything directly controls these main agents; Fleet manages the delegated agents through its own separate system. Everything can have one or more named main agents; one is shown here to explain the interaction. Each stays responsive to the user and delegates heavily. “Coding agents” is the current working term for the dedicated agents they delegate to. Main agent turns have no automatic path to the conversation; outgoing messages pass through the messaging tool.

## Example to explore

1. The user asks Everything to research an idea and make a code change.

2.

3. The main agent uses Fleet MCP to launch and control delegated agents in Fleet instances, using workspace templates and GitHub repositories where needed, while continuing to attend to the user.

4. A subagent reports an intermediate finding. The main agent can act on it without sending a chat message.

5. The user changes direction. Their message interrupts the main agent, which attends to the user promptly and incorporates the new instruction into its coordination of the work.

6. When a question, useful update, or result is ready, the main agent calls the messaging tool.

Fast, responsive attention to the user is a core requirement. The runtime mechanics for interrupting and resuming the main agent still need to be designed.

## Choices still open

- **Interruption mechanics:** How should the runtime interrupt the main agent, handle an in-flight tool call, and resume or revise its work? What happens to delegated tasks during an interruption?

- **Communication:** When should the main agent speak, ask, or stay quiet?

- **Continuity:** How should the main agent organize and retrieve the notes and context it saves in its persistent filesystem?

- **Visibility:** How much delegated activity should the user be able to inspect?

- **Execution:** How many agents are useful, and when should the system create or reuse them?

pages.markdown:
[Back to the concept and high-level map](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_9e931f7ec15c8191a996a3bcaacb8856)

## Main agent harness

**Decision: Pi powers the main agents.** Everything directly controls one or more main agents whose names are chosen by the user using Pi. Fleet manages the delegated agents and their runtimes through its own separate system; Pi is selected only for the main agents.

### User interruption

A user message interrupts the main agent's current execution and is injected into its conversation so the agent can respond promptly. The agent replies through its explicit messaging tool. After replying, it can attempt to resume its previous work or continue according to the user's new direction.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    U["User"]
    subgraph APP["Everything"]
        M["Named main agents powered by Pi"]
    end
    subgraph FLEET["Fleet"]
        F["Orchestration and instance management"]
        A["Delegated agents with Fleet-managed runtimes"]
    end
    U -->|"Messages interrupt the main agent"| M
    M -->|"Explicit messaging tool"| U
    M -->|"Delegate and control through Fleet MCP"| F
    F -->|"Launch and manage"| A
    A -->|"May message the main agent"| F
    F -->|"Deliver message and wake main agent"| M
```

## Kubernetes deployment

Everything will be self-hosted on Kubernetes, starting with five pods.

| Pod | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Keycloak | Authentication and user management for the single user. |
| Everything | Application API, conversation and message handling, Web Push delivery, main-agent management, and Pi running one or more named main agents. |
| UI | Serve the React progressive web app (PWA), styled with Tailwind CSS. |
| Artifact | Nginx serving static artifacts from a persistent PVC shared with the Everything pod. |
| PostgreSQL | Persistent database server with separate databases for Keycloak and Everything. Everything stores main-agent definitions and settings here. |

This is a single-user system. Keycloak provides login; no multi-user authorization or role model is planned.

The Everything pod is the application's core. Its API lets the UI send and retrieve messages and access conversations. The API, main-agent management, and Pi runtime share this pod because they are closely coupled. It also handles Web Push delivery for the installed PWA, as described in [User Surfaces](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_b5de4204a0808191a448e59fce061e9e).

### Persistence and restart behavior

Each main agent has its own folder in the Everything pod, backed by its own persistent volume claim (PVC). Notes, memory, and work files stay in that agent's storage. User-visible artifacts use the shared artifact PVC described below.

For now, Pi sessions use Pi's native JSONL files on persistent disk backed by a PVC. Everything reopens the appropriate session when restoring a main agent after a restart. The initial implementation keeps Pi's existing session persistence; a custom PostgreSQL session adapter is deferred.

All application and agent data must survive pod restarts and replacement. Alongside agent files, this includes conversations, saved messages, agent sessions and stored runtime state, Pi and application configuration, credentials, and Keycloak data. Persistent storage must cover all of this state; it must not rely on a pod's ephemeral filesystem.

Losing an in-flight message during a restart is acceptable. Strict message-delivery guarantees are not required. This exception does not extend to already stored messages, conversations, or other persistent data.

### Database storage

A PostgreSQL container runs in its own pod with a persistent PVC for database files. Keycloak stores its data in a dedicated database on this server. PostgreSQL is supported directly by Keycloak. [Keycloak database documentation](https://www.keycloak.org/server/db)

Everything stores its main-agent definitions, user-chosen names, and settings in a separate application database on the same PostgreSQL server. Everything owns the list of agents and uses their saved definitions to create or restore Pi sessions. An agent's definition persists independently of whether that agent is currently running. Agent names are not hard-coded.

### Artifact serving

A dedicated artifact pod runs Nginx. A shared persistent PVC is mounted into both the Everything pod and the artifact pod. Main agents write HTML files and other static assets to this volume; Nginx reads the same files and serves them to the user. Artifact files survive pod restarts and replacement.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B["User browser or installed PWA"]
    subgraph K8S["Everything on Kubernetes - five starting pods"]
        UI["UI pod / React PWA and Tailwind CSS"]
        KC["Keycloak pod / single-user authentication"]
        PG["PostgreSQL pod / Keycloak and Everything databases"]
        PGV["Persistent PVC for PostgreSQL data"]
        KC <-->|"Store authentication data"| PG
        PG <-->|"Persist database files"| PGV
        subgraph EP["Everything pod"]
            API["Application API / messages and conversations"]
            M["Main-agent management / Pi main agents"]
            API <-->|"Manage and interact with main agents"| M
        end
        API <-->|"Store main-agent definitions and settings"| PG
        ART["Artifact pod / Nginx"]
        H["Shared persistent artifact PVC / HTML and static assets"]
        P["Per-agent PVCs / separate mounted folders"]
        C["Persistent mounts / Pi JSONL sessions, configuration and state"]
        M <-->|"Read and write agent files"| P
        M <-->|"Preserve Pi state"| C
        M -->|"Write artifacts through shared mount"| H
        H -->|"Read artifacts through shared mount"| ART
    end
    UI -->|"Serve the application"| B
    ART -->|"Serve static artifacts"| B
    B <-->|"Sign in"| KC
    B <-->|"Send messages and retrieve conversations through the UI"| API
    M <-->|"Fleet MCP"| F["Fleet / delegated agents and their separate runtimes"]
```

Fleet continues to own delegated-agent execution. The Pi agents in the Everything pod are the main agents only.

## Web app

The React web app is Everything's primary user surface. It uses Tailwind CSS and is served by the UI pod, as described in [Architecture](https://chatgpt.com/space/page_2b6d7736601c8191bdf3ef991520ee7c).

### Visual design and themes

Midnight is Everything's default theme, paired with Signal's grid artwork and the constellation logo. Multiple color themes are a product requirement: the desktop web app and iPhone PWA use shared semantic design tokens for surfaces, text, actions, borders, and other visual roles. Components keep the same layout, typography, and behavior across themes.

The [interactive UI concept](https://everything-ui-concept.solar-tapir-0156.chatgpt.site) includes two dark themes (Midnight and Graphite) and two light themes (Daylight and Sand), with a theme picker and a remembered selection. Carry this token-based approach into the React and Tailwind implementation.

## iPhone progressive web app

**Decision: Everything will support installation on iPhone as a progressive web app (PWA).** This uses the same React application and UI pod. Users add it to their Home Screen through Safari, with Open as Web App enabled. [Apple installation instructions](https://support.apple.com/en-lamr/guide/iphone/iphea86e5236/ios)

### Push notifications

Push notifications are a core requirement for user-facing agent messages and updates, including when the app is closed. On iPhone, users install the app on the Home Screen and explicitly enable notifications from within it. Home Screen Web Push is supported on iOS 16.4 and later and does not require paid Apple Developer Program membership. [WebKit Web Push documentation](https://webkit.org/blog/13878/web-push-for-web-apps-on-ios-and-ipados/)

The Everything backend handles Web Push delivery. Agents continue running on the server while the phone app is closed.
